title: Akka Mahadevi
hook: a silkworm spins its own house from inside itself, and is caught in it: Akka Mahadevi's picture of desire

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mirabai at Dwarka, asking for one last visit to the temple, and leaving only her sari behind. Did you pause at a door for one more look? Day one thousand three hundred sixty.

A silkworm doesn't find its house. It makes it, out of its own body, thread by thread, turning and turning, until the house is finished and the worm is sealed inside. Everything it needed came from within it, and so did the trap. That small, exact picture opens one of the sayings of a woman people called Akka, elder sister. She spoke to Shiva in Kannada, in the south, and her name for him was a flower. Today we meet her.
screen: `A SILKWORM SPINS ITS HOUSE.` → `AKKA, ELDER SISTER.` → `HER NAME FOR GOD WAS A FLOWER.`

segments.voice: Her name is Mahadevi, and people called her Akka, elder sister, so she comes down to us as Akka Mahadevi. She belongs to the Virashaiva, or Lingayat, saints of Karnataka, devotees of Shiva who spoke their faith in short, sharp sayings called vachanas. They're not hymns for a temple choir. They're closer to speech, a person talking straight to God, or about God, in plain Kannada. Her sayings carry her name for Shiva: Chennamallikarjuna. Some readers render it as the beautiful lord, white as jasmine. A god called by the name of a small white flower. Now the silkworm, in paraphrase. The silkworm builds its house lovingly out of itself, and dies tangled in what it wound. So I burn with my heart's wanting. Lord white as jasmine, cut through this greed in me, and show me a way out. Notice first: she doesn't blame the world for trapping her. The thread comes from inside: her own wanting, spun round and round. That's honest, and it's uncomfortable. And she doesn't fix herself, either. She asks him to cut the thread. The way out, in the saying, is his doing, not her cleverness. Then listen to the voice. No priest stands between her and Shiva, no special language. A woman speaks in her own tongue, about her own heart, to a god she calls by the name of a flower. That directness is the gift of the vachanas, and Akka's voice is a sharp one.
screen: `AKKA, ELDER SISTER, SAINT OF SHIVA` · `THE LORD WHITE AS JASMINE` · `THE THREAD COMES FROM INSIDE` · `ASKING HIM TO CUT IT`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: watching one thread. Sit, and let the breath slow. Notice one wanting that's active in you right now. Maybe something small: a snack, a message, a result. Don't fight it and don't follow it. Just watch it the way you'd watch a silkworm turning, round and round. See how it spins. On each out-breath, loosen your grip on it a little. If you pray, you can ask, as Akka did, for help with the thread. The bell holds the time.
Akka Mahadevi. Elder sister, a saint of Shiva who spoke in Kannada vachanas, and called him the lord white as jasmine. Today's word.
Your line: Akka Mahadevi. Today, when a wanting starts spinning, notice the first turn of the thread, and name it. Day one thousand three hundred sixty.

howItsDone: Lingayats and other devotees of Shiva in Karnataka honor Akka Mahadevi among the vachana saints; her sayings are recited, sung and taught, and are read in Kannada and in translation.
